newsitem.title: GERMANY: WW2 German deserters set for "partial" recompense.
newsitem.headline: WW2 German deserters set for "partial" recompense.

text.p: Fifty-two years after the defeat of Nazi Germany, deserters and conscientious objectors looked close on Wednesday to winning long-sought recognition for rejecting Hitler's war and recompense for their persecution.
A majority of deputies on the German parliament's legal affairs committee passed a resolution on their rehabilitation and compensation -- a declaration also likely to win parliamentary approval.

But the leader of a lobby group representing many objectors, Ludwig Baumann, 75, said he was disappointed with what he called a "partial rehabilitation" that stopped short of calling on German justice to lift their guilty verdicts.

"It's not so much compensation we want, but full rehabilitation," Baumann said. "The declaration does not change the fact we can still be regarded as criminals and it does not improve the chances of the guilty verdicts being lifted".
"It's a scandal that we still have criminal records. We suffered the bloodiest judicial persecution in German history. The discrimination continued after the war," Baumann said.
The declaration, in the form of a resolution which parliament will vote on, expresses sympathy for the men's suffering and recognises them as victims of Nazi injustice.
It recalls the plight of many who were condemned to death, executed or sent to concentration camps and grants each victim or victim's family the right to a 7,500-mark payment.

But Baumann said it was marred by one line -- a concession to conservatives which says the declaration does not apply to those who deserted to escape punishment for crimes that would be punishable under law today.
"People can interpret this as they like -- this is a second-class rehabilitation," said Baumann, adding the text gave victims little hope of getting their convictions overturned.

Baumann said the Nazis persecuted between 70,000 and 80,000 men for desertion and as conscientious objectors; 30,000 of these were sentenced to death and 20,000 executed and only about 4,000 survived. Of those about 200 are still alive today.

"We will accept the decision because the survivors are old and sick and need any material help they can get. But we will continue to fight to have our guilty verdicts lifted," said Baumann, who deserted in 1942.
He was sentenced to death and lived on death row for nearly a year before his term was commuted.

A legal expert in Bavaria's conservative Christian Social Union (CSU), Norbert Geis, hailed the declaration because it eschewed blanket rehabilitation. He said this meant "genuine criminals" would not be wrongly rehabilitated.

The decision marked a compromise between between the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) and Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) along with their coalition partners, the CSU and liberal Free Democrats, after years of wrangling.
The environmental Greens were the only party in the committee to object to the text of the declaration and abstain from voting for it.

"The terms of compensation in this case are different from those for other victims of Nazi justice, who are provided for by a federal compensation law," the Greens' legal affairs spokesman Volker Beck said in a statement.
Beck said the victims should be entitled to a pension like other Nazi victims.
